title: Muhammad al-Baqir and Ja'far al-Sadiq
hookLine: Imams of learning in Medina, whose circles, reports say, included Abu Hanifa and Malik

lines: A RING OF STUDENTS IN MEDINA.
ABU HANIFA AND MALIK, REPORTS SAY.
cards: A courtyard in Medina. Students sit on the ground in a ring, some with ink and paper, some just listening hard. Questions about prayer, about inheritance, about what a verse means and what a hadith allows.
At the center sits a descendant of the Prophet, peace be upon him.
Among those who came to circles like this, the reports say, were two men whose names would later be given to whole schools of Sunni law: Abu Hanifa and Malik.
The teachers were a father and son, the son and grandson of Ali Zayn al-Abidin.

teach.h: AL-BAQIR: THE ONE WHO SPLITS IT OPEN.
teach.b: Start with the father, Muhammad, son of Ali Zayn al-Abidin. He is known as al-Baqir. Tradition explains the title as baqir al-ilm, the one who splits knowledge open.

A report kept in Shia sources, and in some Sunni ones, says the Prophet told his companion Jabir that he would live to meet a descendant named Muhammad who would split knowledge open, and asked Jabir to give him greetings.
The reports say Jabir did, as an old man. For Shia Muslims, al-Baqir is the fifth Imam.
Then the son, Ja'far, called al-Sadiq, the truthful. For Shia Muslims he is the sixth Imam, and Twelver Shia law is still called Ja'fari law, after him. But his circle was wide.
Sunni hadith collections, including Sahih Muslim, carry reports that pass through him.

teach.h: ABU HANIFA AND MALIK IN THE RING.
teach.b: Abu Hanifa is reported to have learned from him, and Malik is reported to have said that he never saw anyone better than Ja'far in knowledge and devotion.
One more thread, as the reports tell it: Ja'far's mother descended from Abu Bakr, and Ja'far is reported to have said that Abu Bakr was his ancestor twice over.

So in one Medina courtyard sit threads that Sunni and Shia Muslims would later follow in different directions, and both still honor the teacher at its center. These two did not answer Karbala with swords.

how: Twelver Shia Muslims follow Ja'fari law, named for Ja'far al-Sadiq, and honor al-Baqir and al-Sadiq as the fifth and sixth Imams; Sunni scholars cite reports that pass through them.

o: the one who splits knowledge open
the one who guards the gates of Medina
the one who copies out the Qur'an by hand

games.q: al-Baqir and al-Sadiq — tap the pairs.
p: the one who splits knowledge open

s: Ja'far al-Sadiq is honored only by Shia Muslims
Sunni collections, including Sahih Muslim, carry reports through him, and Malik is reported to have praised him.
al-Baqir was the son of Ali Zayn al-Abidin
the father of Ja'far, and the fifth Imam for Shia Muslims.
al-Baqir and al-Sadiq led armies against the rulers of their day
these two answered with teaching, in a circle of students.

games.q: you're a young scholar in Medina, and you've heard a descendant of the Prophet teaches in a courtyard nearby. what do you do?
o: stay with your own teachers only.
go and sit in his circle.
wait for him to write a book.
games.why: the reports say scholars like Abu Hanifa and Malik came to learn from Ja'far al-Sadiq.

practice: Bring to mind the best teacher you ever had, not the most well-known, but the one who split something open for you: a coach, a grandparent, a book. Remember one thing they taught you that is still growing.
Then name one person whose circle you've never sat in, and what you'd ask them first.

wordCard.voice: Al-Baqir, one who splits knowledge open: the title given to Muhammad, the father of Ja'far al-Sadiq, both teachers in Medina whose circles, reports say, reached Abu Hanifa and Malik. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: one who splits open; tradition explains the title as 'the one who splits knowledge open'.

carryVoice: Your line: the splitting-open of knowledge. A wide circle, honored on both sides. Day eight hundred ninety-four.

sources.ref: Reports of Jabir ibn Abdullah and the Prophet's greeting to al-Baqir (in Shia collections such as al-Kafi, and in some Sunni works)
Sahih Muslim (reports narrated through Ja'far ibn Muhammad, e.g. Jabir's account of the Prophet's farewell pilgrimage)
al-Dhahabi, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' (Malik's praise of Ja'far; Abu Hanifa's study; 'Abu Bakr begot me twice')
